claim: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) form a selective filter that allows the rapid passage of transport factors (TFs) and their cargoes across the nuclear envelope, while blocking the passage of other macromolecules.
source: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) form a selective filter that allows the rapid passage of transport factors (TFs) and their cargoes across the nuclear envelope, while blocking the passage of other macromolecules.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript and general scientific knowledge.

claim: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) containing phenylalanyl-glycyl (FG)-rich repeats line the pore and interact with TFs.
source: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) containing phenylalanyl-glycyl (FG)-rich repeats line the pore and interact with TFs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: FG repeats are highly dynamic IDPs, stabilized by the cellular environment.
source: We show that FG repeats are highly dynamic IDPs, stabilized by the cellular environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR measurements showing disorder and dynamics in cellular milieu, as shown in Figure 1 and related data.

claim: The rapid motion of FG motifs allows them to exchange on and off TFs extremely quickly through transient interactions.
source: Fast transport of TFs is supported because the rapid motion of FG motifs allows them to exchange on and off TFs extremely quickly through transient interactions.
evidence: This is supported by NMR relaxation data showing rapid dynamics and titration experiments showing fast exchange kinetics.

claim: TFs uniquely carry multiple pockets for FG repeats, allowing them to form the many frequent interactions needed for specific passage between FG repeats to cross the NPC.
source: Because TFs uniquely carry multiple pockets for FG repeats, only they can form the many frequent interactions needed for specific passage between FG repeats to cross the NPC.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge of TFs and the multivalent binding data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The entire process of transport factor (TF) docking, passage and release across the NPC takes only a few milliseconds.
source: Transport is rapid and reversible, with the entire process of transport factor (TF) docking, passage and release across the NPC taking only a few milliseconds (Strawn et al., 2004; Hulsmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The NPC consists of a ∼30-nm diameter central channel filled with phenylalanyl-glycyl-repeat-rich nucleoporins (FG Nups) which provide the selective filter.
source: The NPC consists of a ∼30-nm diameter central channel filled with phenylalanyl-glycyl-repeat-rich nucleoporins (FG Nups) which provide the selective filter.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the NPC.

claim: Depletion or deletion of the FG Nups results in leaky, non-selective barriers.
source: Depletion or deletion of the FG Nups results in leaky, non-selective barriers (Strawn et al., 2004; Di Nunzio et al., 2012; Hulsmann et al., 2012; Funasaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: FG domains in isolation facilitate selective passage of TFs through nanopores.
source: Moreover, the FG domains in isolation facilitate selective passage of TFs through nanopores (Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Kowalczyk et al., 2011) or accumulation in hydrogels (Frey et al., 2006; Frey and Görlich, 2007; Schmidt and Gorlich, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: TF interaction with FG repeats reduces the diffusional barrier to enable selective transport.
source: It is generally accepted that TF interaction with FG repeats reduce the diffusional barrier to enable selective transport (Vasu and Forbes, 2001; Rout et al., 2003; Suntharalingam and Wente, 2003; Zeitler and Weis, 2004), though the molecular mechanism of TF passage through the NPC remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a generally accepted view in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: TFs can change the height of FG brushes on planar surfaces.
source: Mesoscale observations of TF-FG repeat interactions in vitro have shown that TFs can change the height of FG brushes on planar surfaces (Lim et al., 2007; Eisele et al., 2010; Kapinos et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2015), modulate the transport of inert cargo (Lowe et al., 2015), assemble with FG Nups into large assemblies (Lowe et al., 2015), and inhibit amyloid hydrogel formation observed for some FG Nups (Milles et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental observations.

claim: FG-N and FSFG-K fragments are fully disordered, with no propensity for secondary structure in E. coli cells.
source: Deviations of chemical shift values in cell (Escherichia coli) from predicted (colored bars) showing that FG-N and FSFG-K fragments are fully disordered, with no propensity for secondary structure.
evidence: This is directly supported by NMR chemical shift data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FG-N and FSFG-K constructs show significant interactions with the cellular milieu and exhibit very rapid motions.
source: The FG-N and FSFG-K constructs show significant interactions with the cellular milieu and exhibit very rapid motions.
evidence: This is supported by R2/R1 ratios and nOe data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FG Nups were fully disordered and highly dynamic in all cellular milieu tested.
source: FG Nups were fully disordered and highly dynamic in all cellular milieu tested.
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift and relaxation measurements in various cellular environments.

claim: The degree of secondary structure is near zero for all residues in FG-N and FSFG-K constructs in all conditions tested.
source: The degree of secondary structure quantified in this way is near zero for all residues in FG-N and FSFG-K constructs in all conditions tested (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Eliezer, 2009).
evidence: This is directly measured from NMR chemical shift data shown in figures.

claim: FG-N forms a hydrogel-like material in buffer alone.
source: Under these conditions, dynamic light scattering and NMR measurements indicate that FG-N forms a hydrogel-like material (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by dynamic light scattering and NMR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: When FG-N constructs are observed by NMR inside a living cell, or in the presence of cell lysates or mimics, there is no appearance of high molecular weight components.
source: However, when FG-N constructs are observed by NMR inside a living cell, or in the presence of cell lysates or mimics, there is no appearance of high molecular weight components—NMR spectra of FG-N constructs in living E. coli did not change with time over more than 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is directly observed in NMR spectra over time shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The cellular milieu is a strong inhibitor of intermolecular FG repeat aggregation.
source: These data indicate that the cellular milieu is a strong inhibitor of intermolecular FG repeat aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FG-N does not aggregate in cellular milieu but does in buffer alone.

claim: The state of FG repeats in the experimental system is highly dynamic, as has been reported in vivo.
source: The state of FG repeats in our system is therefore highly dynamic, as has been reported in vivo (Mattheyses et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' NMR data and cited previous in vivo observations.

claim: NMR relaxation properties of FG Nups are significantly different between buffer alone and a protein-rich environment.
source: NMR relaxation properties of FG Nups are significantly different between buffer alone and a protein-rich environment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the R2/R1 and nOe data in Figure 1C.

claim: Large increases in R2/R1 were measured, indicative of transient spectral changes on interaction between the constructs and the cellular milieu.
source: We measured large increases in R2/R1, indicative of transient spectral changes on interaction between the constructs and the cellular milieu (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly measured from NMR relaxation experiments shown in figures.

claim: The increases in R2/R1 were not seen upon increasing viscosity or crowding by inert agents.
source: The increases in R2/R1 were not seen upon increasing viscosity or crowding by inert agents (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), indicating that these changes result from weak binding of the FG repeats to the proteinaceous milieu as suggested by previous studies (Tetenbaum-Novatt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown by control experiments with various crowding agents in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The phenylalanines and their adjacent residues show the primary interactions with the cellular milieu, with the greatest increases in R2/R1, while the spacer sequences remained relatively unaffected.
source: The phenylalanines and their adjacent residues show the primary interactions, with the greatest increases in R2/R1, while the spacer sequences remained relatively unaffected.
evidence: This is observed in the sequence-specific R2/R1 data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nuclear Overhauser effect (nOe) data show that the FG-N are highly mobile and flexible.
source: The nuclear Overhauser effect (nOe) data show that the FG-N are highly mobile and flexible (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating no sequence-specific compaction, folding, or molten globule formation (Uversky, 2009; Theillet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly measured from nOe experiments shown in figures.

claim: The cellular milieu is in a state of constant, non-specific, dynamic interaction with the FG repeats.
source: The cellular milieu is thus in a state of constant, non-specific, dynamic interaction with the FG repeats.
evidence: This is inferred from the R2/R1 and nOe data showing transient interactions without structural changes.

claim: Interactions of FG repeats with the cellular milieu stabilize the unfolded state by engaging the hydrophobic phenylalanines in transient interactions that decrease their contact with water.
source: Our results suggest that interactions of FG repeats with the cellular milieu stabilize the unfolded state by engaging the hydrophobic phenylalanines in transient interactions that decrease their contact with the water, reducing the driving force for hydrophobic collapse and amyloid formation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the observed data and previous knowledge about hydrophobic interactions.

claim: Mutation of the Fs to more hydrophilic residues inhibits aggregation.
source: This is consistent with previous work that demonstrated that mutation of the Fs to more hydrophilic residues inhibits aggregation (Frey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Exchange with the cellular milieu maintains the FG Nups in a highly dynamic, disordered state by inhibiting the intramolecular interactions that lead to aggregation in buffer.
source: Thus, exchange with the cellular milieu maintains the FG Nups in a highly dynamic, disordered state by inhibiting the intramolecular interactions that lead to aggregation in buffer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of FG Nup behavior in cellular milieu versus buffer.

claim: FG residues bind to hydrophobic pockets on TFs.
source: It has long been established using crystallographic, computational, and NMR approaches that FG residues bind to hydrophobic pockets on TFs (reviewed in Stewart, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to a review.

claim: The FG repeat-TF interactions are fully reversible.
source: By monitoring the recovery of the NMR spectral characteristics on dilution of Kap95, the interacting TF, we showed that the FG repeat-TF interactions are fully reversible in our system (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dilution experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Although the phenylalanine repeats themselves are attenuated upon Kap95 interaction, the majority of peaks are minimally affected, showing that the corresponding residues remain disordered and dynamic.
source: Strikingly, although the phenylalanine repeats themselves are attenuated upon Kap95 interaction, the majority of peaks are minimally affected, showing that the corresponding residues remain disordered and dynamic (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the HSQC titration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The spacer regions are highly mobile even within the interacting state.
source: The spacer regions are thus highly mobile even within the interacting state.
evidence: This is inferred from the minimal attenuation of spacer region peaks upon TF binding.

claim: K332 shows no attenuation and thus this residue remains flexible both in free and when bound to TF.
source: An extreme of this observation is seen for K332, which shows no attenuation (left subpanel in Figure 2A, lowest trace Figure 2C), and thus this residue remains flexible both in free and when bound to TF.
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A striking periodic pattern of minimal attenuation for most residues and significant attenuation for FG repeats was observed when examining attenuation as a function of residue number.
source: When we examined attenuation as a function of residue number, we observed a striking periodic pattern of minimal attenuation for most residues and significant attenuation for FG repeats (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the attenuation plot in Figure 2B.

claim: The degree of signal attenuation falls off relatively uniformly at both sides of each FG repeat, consistent with the transient binding of individual FG residues.
source: The degree of signal attenuation falls off relatively uniformly at both sides of each FG repeat, consistent with the transient binding of individual FG residues, with the remaining residues remaining fully disordered and highly dynamic.
evidence: This is observed in the attenuation data and interpreted as evidence for transient binding.

claim: No major state change of spacers resulting from TF addition was observed, such as caused by the formation or breakage of secondary structure, or gel/sol transitions.
source: We did not observe any major state change of spacers resulting from TF addition, such as caused by the formation or breakage of secondary structure, or gel/sol transitions (Ader et al., 2010; Labokha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a negative result from the NMR data, indicating no structural changes upon TF binding.

claim: The binding interface between FG Nups and TFs at each interacting site is small—just the 2–4 residues surrounding the FG repeat itself.
source: We observe that the binding interface between FG Nups and TFs at each interacting site is small—just the 2–4 residues surrounding the FG repeat itself—and the residues that do not interact directly with the TF sites remain highly mobile and dynamic.
evidence: This is inferred from the localized attenuation pattern around FG repeats in the NMR data.

claim: The size of the binding interface is consistent with other known transient interactions.
source: The size of the binding interface is consistent with other known transient interactions (Clackson and Wells, 1995; Morrison et al., 2003; Tompa et al., 2009; Dixon et al., 2011; Ozbabacan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on transient protein interactions.

claim: A minimum effective affinity of Kap95 for the FSFG-K was estimated from a titration observing 15N R2, with the true Kd greater than 36 μM.
source: We estimated a minimum effective affinity of Kap95 for the FSFG-K from a titration observing 15N R2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Su et al., 2007). The true Kd is greater than 36 μM, fully consistent with rapid, reversible transport.
evidence: This is derived from R2 titration experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Interaction or binding while remaining primarily disordered is highly unusual, as many functional IDPs are believed to adopt significant secondary structure formation upon interaction.
source: Interaction or binding while remaining primarily disordered is highly unusual, as many functional IDPs are believed to adopt significant secondary structure formation upon interaction (Wright and Dyson, 2009; Uversky and Dunker, 2013), which we do not see here.
evidence: This contrasts the observed behavior with typical IDP behavior cited in the literature.

claim: The behavior of FG Nups is reminiscent of that proposed for random fuzzy complexes, in which one partner remains dynamically disordered and transient interactions predominate during selective recognition.
source: This behavior is reminiscent of that proposed for random fuzzy complexes, in which one partner remains dynamically disordered and transient interactions predominate during selective recognition (Sigalov, 2011; Fuxreiter and Tompa, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: There are multiple transport routes across the NPC, with FG Nups arranged in a variety of geometries.
source: Many observations suggest that there are multiple transport routes across the NPC, with FG Nups arranged in a variety of geometries (Akey and Radermacher, 1993; Goldberg and Allen, 1996; Gant et al., 1998; Kiseleva et al., 2004; Alber et al., 2007; Burns and Wente, 2012; Laba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: Essentially no change in chemical shifts and only modest changes in linewidth were found upon attachment to the p53 tetramerization domain.
source: We found essentially no change in chemical shifts and only modest changes in linewidth upon attachment to the p53 tetramerization domain (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR spectra comparing monomeric and tetrameric constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: FG Nups remain dynamic IDPs even in large complexes.
source: Any ordered protein of this size (∼120 kDa) would be invisible using our NMR experiments, demonstrating that FG Nups remain dynamic IDPs even in large complexes, as previously measured for other large IDPs (Kosol et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of NMR signals for the large tetrameric constructs.

claim: The largest constructs have a diameter measured by dynamic light scattering of 13 nm, a significant fraction of the 30-nm diameter of the NPC.
source: Notably, our largest constructs have a diameter measured by dynamic light scattering of 13 nm (Figure 3B), a significant fraction of the 30-nm diameter of the NPC.
evidence: This is directly measured by dynamic light scattering shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The behavior of a given FG repeat is not affected strongly by the number or type of other FG repeats surrounding it.
source: Our results reveal that the behavior of a given FG repeat is not affected strongly by the number or type of other FG repeats surrounding it (i.e., no 'emergent properties').
evidence: This is concluded from comparing NMR data of different constructs with varying FG compositions and arrangements.

claim: There are no significant FG–FG interactions.
source: Our results also strongly indicate that there are no significant FG–FG interactions, as interactions between different types of FGs should impact their average environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of chemical shift changes when different FG types are combined.

claim: Extremely weak, dynamic interactions may occur between FG repeats, and such interactions may modulate the long distance distribution of FG repeat regions in the NPC.
source: However, we cannot completely exclude that extremely weak, dynamic interactions can occur between FG repeats, and indeed such interactions may modulate the long distance distribution of FG repeat regions in the NPC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the measurements.

claim: The FG Nups remain a highly dynamic fluid even at sizes, arrangements, and packing densities commensurate with the NPC.
source: The FG Nups thus remain a highly dynamic fluid even at sizes, arrangements, and packing densities commensurate with the NPC.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data on various constructs including large tetrameric assemblies.

claim: The same pattern of rapid exchange of the FG residues with TF binding sites while the spacer regions remain highly mobile was observed in all environments studied and with all constructs tested.
source: We observed the same pattern of rapid exchange of the FG residues with TF binding sites while the spacer regions remain highly mobile in all environments studied and with all constructs tested, showing the robustness of our findings (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown across multiple constructs and conditions in Figure 4.

claim: Even when densely packed and in mixed flavors as in the NPC, the FG repeat regions studied remain fully disordered and highly dynamic.
source: We show that, even when densely packed and in mixed flavors as in the NPC, the FG repeat regions studied here remain fully disordered and highly dynamic.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR data on various constructs including tetrameric assemblies with mixed FG types.

claim: FSFG-K is highly soluble and non-cohesive, while FG-N in buffer is highly cohesive, a prototypical hydrogel-forming FG Nup.
source: The two domains studied represent the extreme behaviors observed for FG Nups in vitro (Patel et al., 2007; Ader et al., 2010; Yamada et al., 2010): FSFG-K is highly soluble and non-cohesive, while FG-N in buffer is highly cohesive, a prototypical hydrogel-forming FG Nup.
evidence: This is established by previous work cited and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claim: The data are inconsistent with any hydrogel state in cellular milieu.
source: It is clearly possible to make FG repeats aggregate (Figure 1—figure supplements 4, 5) (Ader et al., 2010), as has been demonstrated for many proteins (Goldschmidt et al., 2010). However, our data are inconsistent with any such hydrogel state in cellular milieu (Frey et al., 2006; Labokha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data showing no aggregation in cellular milieu.

claim: Re-arrangements of internal non-covalent crosslinks within hydrogels are on slow (second to minute) timescales, long enough to form a solid gel resistant to deformation, and too slow for solution NMR analysis.
source: Re-arrangements of internal non-covalent crosslinks within hydrogels are on slow (second to minute) timescales, long enough to form a solid gel resistant to deformation, and too slow for solution NMR analysis (Ader et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of hydrogel dynamics and NMR timescales, supported by citation.

claim: FG repeat regions form a highly dynamic phase, consistent with the rapid rates of nuclear transport.
source: Instead of such a highly internally interacting, slowly moving gel, our results demonstrate that FG repeat regions form a highly dynamic phase, consistent with the rapid rates of nuclear transport.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data showing rapid dynamics and compared to known transport rates.

claim: A highly dynamic, fluid state for FG repeats in vivo is in agreement with measurements of the living NPC.
source: A highly dynamic, fluid state for FG repeats in vivo is in agreement with measurements of the living NPC (Atkinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous in vivo measurements.

claim: FG Nups do not appear to form a molten globule or collapsed state, instead behaving as a fully disordered IDP.
source: FG Nups do not appear to form a molten globule or collapsed state, as has also been proposed (Yamada et al., 2010), instead behaving as a fully disordered IDP (Rout et al., 2003; Lim et al., 2006; Lim and Deng, 2009; Atkinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data showing no evidence of compaction or secondary structure.

claim: FG repeats do not appear to populate more folded states either inter- or intra-molecularly upon interaction with either TFs or other FG Nups.
source: Our results also allow us to distinguish their IDP class (Uversky, 2011; van der Lee et al., 2014). FG repeats do not appear to populate more folded states either inter- or intra-molecularly upon interaction with either TFs or other FG Nups (Wright and Dyson, 2009; Yamada et al., 2010; Han et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: This is concluded from the chemical shift data showing no secondary structure formation upon binding.

claim: IDP mobility may be a key ingredient in nuclear transport.
source: Instead, FG repeats lack any secondary structure, even when interacting with cognate binding partners, indicating that IDP mobility may be a key ingredient in nuclear transport.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the observed dynamics and disorder.

claim: The importance of the cellular environment for determining the behavior of the FG Nups is highlighted because multiple weak interactions with cellular components stabilize the FG Nups in a disordered state.
source: Our results highlight the importance of the cellular environment for determining the behavior of the FG Nups because multiple weak interactions with cellular components stabilize the FG Nups in a disordered state.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing FG Nup behavior in cellular milieu versus buffer.

claim: The selectivity of the NPC is maintained by both non-specific and specific cellular interactions.
source: We propose that the selectivity of the NPC is thus maintained by both non-specific and specific cellular interactions, consistent with recent work demonstrating that FG permeability barrier is modulated by TFs (Lim et al., 2007; Eisele et al., 2010; Milles et al., 2013; Kapinos et al., 2014; Lowe et al., 2015; Wagner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the authors' data and cited previous work.

claim: The modulation of permeability of FG brush behavior by TFs is not a result of structural changes of the FG Nups, but must result instead from the rapid, multivalent interactions of TFs with FG repeats.
source: We show that the modulation of permeability of FG brush behavior by TFs is not a result of structural changes of the FG Nups, but must result instead from the rapid, multivalent interactions of TFs with FG repeats (Tetenbaum-Novatt et al., 2012; Schleicher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of structural changes observed upon TF binding.

claim: FG repeats being highly dynamic tethered IDPs implies that they must form entropic bristles around their tether site.
source: Our data, strongly supporting that FG repeats are highly dynamic tethered IDPs, imply that they must form entropic bristles (i.e., strongly sterically hindered regions) around their tether site (the central channel of the NPC) (Rout et al., 2003; Strawn et al., 2004; Lim et al., 2006, 2007; Lim and Deng, 2009; Tetenbaum-Novatt and Rout, 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on polymer physics principles applied to the observed IDP behavior.

claim: The entropic hindrance increases with increasing size of the passing macromolecules; hence, small proteins can pass more easily than large ones.
source: This hindrance increases with increasing size of the passing macromolecules; hence, small proteins can pass more easily than large ones (Tetenbaum-Novatt and Rout, 2010).
evidence: This is based on polymer physics principles and cited previous work.

claim: Larger nonspecific macromolecules interact with the FG repeats with insufficient frequency to overcome the entropic barrier of the FG repeats' polymer bristle structure, thus being effectively excluded.
source: These larger nonspecific macromolecules interact with the FG repeats with insufficient frequency to overcome the entropic barrier of the FG repeats' polymer bristle structure, thus being effectively excluded (Tetenbaum-Novatt and Rout, 2010; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the observed weak interactions and polymer physics.

claim: TFs have sufficient interaction frequency to overcome the entropic barrier.
source: TFs, however, have sufficient interaction frequency to do so—the original tenet of the 'virtual gating' idea, now delineated at the atomic scale by these results.
evidence: This is concluded from the observed multivalent, rapid interactions of TFs with FG repeats.

claim: FG disorder is critical to the speed of selective nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: Our results suggest that FG disorder is critical to the speed of selective nucleocytoplasmic transport.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the observed dynamics and binding kinetics.

claim: IDPs are able to engage far more rapidly than most ordered proteins.
source: IDPs are able to engage far more rapidly than most ordered proteins (Zhou, 2012), allowing for high on and off rates while maintaining selectivity.
evidence: This is based on cited knowledge about IDP binding kinetics.

claim: The interaction of FG Nups with TFs is extraordinarily rapid, with each FG motif in extremely fast exchange with TFs.
source: For FGs in particular, several key lines of evidence indicate that the interaction of FG Nups with TFs is extraordinarily rapid, that is, each FG motif is in extremely fast exchange with TFs.
evidence: This is concluded from the NMR data showing fast exchange kinetics.

claim: The binding interface is only 2–4 amino acids (the FG repeat itself).
source: We have directly shown that the binding interface is only 2–4 amino acids (the FG repeat itself).
evidence: This is directly observed from the localized attenuation in NMR titration experiments.

claim: The buried surface area of the FG-TF interaction is <1000 Å2, consistent with other known transient interactions.
source: The buried surface area of this interaction is <1000 Å2, consistent with other known transient interactions (Clackson and Wells, 1995; Tompa et al., 2009; Dixon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is estimated from the small binding interface and compared to cited literature values.

claim: Within the NPC, a TF is able to rapidly diffuse, engaging transiently with multiple FG motifs across different FG Nups.
source: Within the NPC, a TF is able to rapidly diffuse, engaging transiently with multiple FG motifs across different FG Nups.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed rapid, transient interactions and multivalent binding capacity of TFs.

claim: The association rate of TFs with individual FG motifs is very fast because the FGs move very rapidly and the TF has multiple binding pockets available for interaction.
source: The association rate of TFs with individual FG motifs is very fast because the FGs move very rapidly and the TF has multiple binding pockets available for interaction (Bayliss et al., 2000, 2002; Bednenko et al., 2003; Isgro and Schulten, 2005, 2007; Liu and Stewart, 2005).
evidence: This is based on the observed dynamics and structural knowledge of TFs from cited literature.

claim: The dynamics of FG-TF interaction are extraordinarily rapid.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the dynamics of FG-TF interaction are extraordinarily rapid.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of NMR evidence showing fast exchange and rapid dynamics.

claim: The interaction can be strong enough to be selective, and yet remain extremely fast, allowing rapid transit through the NPC.
source: As a result, the interaction can be strong enough to be selective, and yet remain extremely fast, allowing rapid transit through the NPC.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the measured affinity and kinetics.

claim: It is the quantity, rather than quality, of interactions possible per molecule with FG repeats that distinguishes a TF from other macromolecules.
source: In essence, it is the quantity, rather than quality, of interactions possible per molecule with FG repeats that distinguishes a TF from other macromolecules (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion based on the multivalent binding observed and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Transient non-specific interactions of the FG repeats with their milieu help maintain the disordered and dynamic nature of the barrier.
source: Transient non-specific interactions of the FG repeats with their milieu help maintain the disordered and dynamic nature of the barrier.
evidence: This is concluded from the R2/R1 data showing interactions with cellular milieu that prevent aggregation.

claim: Non-specific interactions are not strong enough for non-specific macromolecules to overcome the FG Nups' diffusion barrier.
source: Given the low sequence and structural complexity of the FG repeats, such non-specific interactions are to be expected but are not strong enough for these non-specific macromolecules to overcome the FG Nups' diffusion barrier (Rout et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the weak, transient nature of non-specific interactions observed.

claim: TFs bind specifically to the FG motifs through pockets tuned for this purpose while leaving the spacers between the motifs highly mobile.
source: In contrast, TFs bind specifically to the FG motifs through pockets tuned for this purpose (Stewart, 2003, 2006) while leaving the spacers between the motifs highly mobile.
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR data and supported by structural knowledge from citations.

claim: The barrier to non-specific passage formed by a dense fluid of FG repeats in the NPC remains fully intact, regardless of even large TF fluxes.
source: The fact that the spacers—and the FG repeats as a whole—remain fully mobile even when interacting with a TF also means that the barrier to non-specific passage formed by a dense fluid of FG repeats in the NPC remains fully intact, regardless of even large TF fluxes (a significant issue with models that invoke state changes, which our results and model circumvent).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the observed maintenance of disorder upon TF binding.

claim: Nsp1 is the most tested and characterized FG Nup which has been shown in vitro to mimic transport faithfully.
source: We studied Nsp1, the most tested and characterized FG Nup which has been shown in vitro to mimic transport faithfully (Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Hulsmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The isolated N-terminal domain of Nsp1 forms selective hydrogels in vitro.
source: The isolated N-terminal domain forms selective hydrogels in vitro (Ader et al., 2010) and is able to replace Nup98-FG domain in reconstituted Xenopus nuclei to provide the primary barrier enabling selective transport (Hulsmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.
